questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Alcohols: identification of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols
questions.question: Which of the following alcohols gives turbidity immediately at room temperature when treated with Lucas reagent?

solution.key_concept: Lucas test (conc. $HCl$ + anhydrous $ZnCl_2$) proceeds by an $S_N1$-type path, so the reactivity order is 3° > 2° > 1°.
steps: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol, $(CH_3)_3COH$, is a tertiary alcohol.
It forms the most stable (3°) carbocation, so the insoluble alkyl chloride separates at once as turbidity.
Propan-2-ol (2°) takes about 5 minutes. Ethanol and propan-1-ol (1°) give no turbidity at room temperature.
solution.why_not_others: Ethanol and propan-1-ol are primary and react only on heating. Propan-2-ol is secondary and gives turbidity only within about 5 minutes.
solution.common_trap: Picking propan-2-ol because it reacts at room temperature. It does, but not immediately.
solution.time_saving_tip: Immediate turbidity in the Lucas test means look for a carbinol carbon bonded to three carbons.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Alcohols: identification of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols
questions.question: An alcohol of molecular formula $C_4H_{10}O$ gives a ketone when its vapours are passed over heated copper at 573 K. The alcohol is

solution.key_concept: Over Cu at 573 K, a 1° alcohol gives an aldehyde, a 2° alcohol gives a ketone and a 3° alcohol gives an alkene.
steps: Formation of a ketone shows that the alcohol is secondary.
Among the $C_4H_{10}O$ isomers listed, only butan-2-ol, $CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_3$, is secondary.
It is dehydrogenated to butanone.
solution.why_not_others: Butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are primary and give aldehydes. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary and gives 2-methylpropene.
solution.common_trap: Expecting the tertiary alcohol to give a ketone. Its carbinol carbon has no H, so it dehydrates to an alkene instead.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Alcohols: identification of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols
questions.question: An alcohol X ($C_4H_{10}O$) gives turbidity immediately with Lucas reagent at room temperature. What is the main product when the vapours of X are passed over heated copper at 573 K?

solution.key_concept: Immediate Lucas turbidity identifies a 3° alcohol. A 3° alcohol undergoes dehydration over Cu at 573 K.
steps: The only tertiary alcohol with formula $C_4H_{10}O$ is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $(CH_3)_3COH$.
Its carbinol carbon has no H, so dehydrogenation is not possible.
Over Cu at 573 K it loses water and gives $(CH_3)_2C=CH_2$, which is 2-methylpropene.
solution.why_not_others: 2-Methylpropanal and butanal would come from primary alcohols. Butanone would come from butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol, which gives turbidity only after about 5 minutes.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that Cu at 573 K always gives a carbonyl compound. For 3° alcohols the product is an alkene.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Alcohols: identification of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Tertiary alcohols give turbidity immediately with Lucas reagent at room temperature.
statements.R: Tertiary alcohols react with conc. $HCl$/anhydrous $ZnCl_2$ through the most stable carbocation, and the insoluble alkyl chloride formed separates out.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The Lucas test follows an $S_N1$-type path, and the rate depends on carbocation stability.
steps: A is true: 3° alcohols show turbidity at once.
R is true: a 3° carbocation forms fastest, and the alkyl chloride produced is insoluble, which causes the turbidity.
R explains both why the reaction is fast and why turbidity appears, so it correctly explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are factually correct, which rules out options 3 and 4. R directly accounts for A, which rules out option 2.
solution.common_trap: Thinking the turbidity comes from $ZnCl_2$. It is actually due to the insoluble alkyl chloride.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Alcohols: identification of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Oxidation of propan-1-ol with PCC stops at propanal and does not give propanoic acid.
statements.II: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is readily oxidised by mild oxidising agents to a ketone because its carbinol carbon carries one hydrogen atom.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: PCC oxidises a 1° alcohol only as far as the aldehyde. A 3° alcohol resists mild oxidation because its carbinol carbon has no H.
steps: Statement I: propan-1-ol is a 1° alcohol, and PCC stops at the aldehyde stage, giving propanal. Statement I is correct.
Statement II: in 2-methylpropan-2-ol the carbinol carbon is bonded to three $CH_3$ groups and OH, so it has no H.
Because it has no H on the carbinol carbon, it is not oxidised by mild oxidants. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II misidentifies the structure (the carbinol carbon has no H) and wrongly claims that a ketone is formed. Statement I is correct as written.
solution.common_trap: Confusing 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3°) with butan-2-ol (2°), which is oxidised to a ketone.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Mechanism of dehydration of alcohols
questions.question: In the acid-catalysed dehydration of a tertiary alcohol, the rate-determining step is
options: Loss of a β-proton to form the alkene
Loss of a water molecule to form a carbocation

solution.key_concept: E1 dehydration has three steps: protonation (fast), carbocation formation (slow) and deprotonation.
steps: Step 1, fast protonation of OH, converts it into a good leaving group ($H_2O$).
Step 2, loss of $H_2O$ to give a carbocation, is slow and therefore rate-determining.
Step 3 is loss of a β-proton to give the alkene, which also regenerates the acid.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Loss of a water molecule to form a carbocation
solution.why_not_others: Protonation is fast. Deprotonation and regeneration of the catalyst occur after the slow step.
solution.common_trap: Choosing protonation because it is the first step. The first step is not necessarily the slowest.
solution.time_saving_tip: Since ease of dehydration follows carbocation stability, the slow step must be the one that forms the carbocation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Mechanism of dehydration of alcohols
questions.question: Which set of conditions converts ethanol mainly into diethyl ether?

solution.key_concept: Ethanol dehydrates intramolecularly to an alkene at 443 K but intermolecularly to an ether at 413 K when excess alcohol is used.
steps: At 413 K with excess ethanol, a second ethanol molecule attacks the protonated alcohol by an $S_N2$ path.
Water is eliminated, giving $C_2H_5OC_2H_5$.
At 443 K the same acid gives ethene instead.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Excess ethanol with $H_2SO_4$ at 413 K
solution.why_not_others: Conc. $H_2SO_4$ at 443 K gives ethene. 20% $H_3PO_4$ at 358 K is the condition used for 3° alcohols. Cu at 573 K dehydrogenates ethanol to ethanal.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the two temperatures: 413 K gives the ether, 443 K gives the alkene.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember that the lower temperature (413 K) gives the ether and the higher temperature (443 K) gives the alkene.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Mechanism of dehydration of alcohols
questions.question: What is the major product formed when 2-methylbutan-2-ol is heated with dilute phosphoric acid?

solution.key_concept: E1 dehydration follows the Saytzeff rule: the more substituted alkene is the major product.
steps: Loss of water from $(CH_3)_2C(OH)CH_2CH_3$ gives the 3° carbocation $(CH_3)_2C^+CH_2CH_3$.
β-Protons are available on the $CH_3$ groups and on the $CH_2$ group.
Loss of H from the $CH_2$ group gives the trisubstituted alkene $(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_3$, which is the major product.
solution.why_not_others: 2-Methylbut-1-ene is the less substituted, minor product. 3-Methylbut-1-ene and pent-2-ene have skeletons that cannot arise from this 3° carbocation.
solution.common_trap: Choosing the terminal alkene because more β-hydrogens are available on the methyl groups.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Mechanism of dehydration of alcohols
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Step 1 of acid-catalysed dehydration of an alcohol

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Step 2 of acid-catalysed dehydration of an alcohol

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Step 3 of acid-catalysed dehydration of an alcohol

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Heating excess ethanol with $H_2SO_4$ at 413 K

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Slow loss of $H_2O$ giving a carbocation

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: $S_N2$ attack by a second alcohol molecule giving an ether

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Loss of a β-proton giving an alkene

solution.key_concept: The dehydration mechanism is protonation, then carbocation formation (rate-determining), then deprotonation. At 413 K with excess ethanol, ether formation occurs by $S_N2$.
steps: A: protonation of OH is fast, so A-III.
B: loss of water to give the carbocation is the slow step, so B-I.
C: removal of a β-proton gives the alkene, so C-IV.
D: excess ethanol at 413 K gives diethyl ether by $S_N2$ attack, so D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps protonation and carbocation formation. Option 2 places deprotonation before carbocation formation. Option 3 assigns ether formation to step 1.
solution.common_trap: Thinking protonation is the slow step simply because it comes first.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Mechanism of dehydration of alcohols
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols are correct?

statements.A: The ease of dehydration follows the order 3° > 2° > 1°.
statements.B: The acid is consumed in the reaction and is not regenerated.
statements.C: When two alkenes are possible, the more substituted alkene is the major product.
statements.D: The carbocation intermediate may undergo a 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shift, giving a rearranged alkene.
statements.E: Tertiary alcohols require conc. $H_2SO_4$ at 443 K, while ethanol dehydrates with 20% $H_3PO_4$ at 358 K.

solution.key_concept: Dehydration rates follow carbocation stability, the acid acts as a catalyst, the Saytzeff rule applies and rearrangements are possible.
steps: A is true: the order matches carbocation stability.
B is false: the acid is a catalyst and is regenerated at the end.
C is true: this is the Saytzeff rule.
D is true: carbocations can rearrange by 1,2-H or 1,2-$CH_3$ shifts.
E is false: the conditions are reversed. Ethanol needs conc. $H_2SO_4$ at 443 K, while 3° alcohols need only 20% $H_3PO_4$ at about 358 K.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options 1 and 4 include a false statement (B or E). Option 2 leaves out the true statement D.
solution.common_trap: Reversing the dehydration conditions: the more reactive 3° alcohol needs the milder conditions.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Phenols: acidic nature
questions.question: Phenol does NOT react with which of the following?

solution.key_concept: Phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid but is acidic enough to react with active metals and strong bases.
steps: Phenol reacts with Na to liberate $H_2$.
Phenol is neutralised by $NaOH$ or $KOH$ to form phenoxide.
Because phenol is weaker than $H_2CO_3$, it cannot decompose $NaHCO_3$, so no $CO_2$ is evolved.
solution.why_not_others: Sodium, NaOH and KOH all react with phenol, as described above.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that every acidic OH compound liberates $CO_2$ from $NaHCO_3$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Effervescence with $NaHCO_3$ points to a carboxylic acid, not ordinary phenol.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Phenols: acidic nature
questions.question: The correct decreasing order of acidic strength is

solution.key_concept: An ortho or para $-NO_2$ group acts by the -R effect, while a meta $-NO_2$ acts only by the -I effect. Intramolecular H-bonding slightly weakens the ortho isomer.
steps: The $pK_a$ values are: p-nitrophenol 7.1, o-nitrophenol 7.2, m-nitrophenol 8.3, phenol 10.0.
A lower $pK_a$ means a stronger acid.
Therefore the order is p > o > m > phenol.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 ignores the effect of intramolecular H-bonding in the ortho isomer. Options 2 and 3 overrate the meta isomer, which lacks the -R effect.
solution.common_trap: Placing o-nitrophenol above the para isomer because the nitro group is closer to OH.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Phenols: acidic nature
questions.question: Which of the following is the least acidic?

solution.key_concept: Electron-donating groups decrease the acidity of phenol, while electron-withdrawing groups increase it.
steps: The $-CH_3$ group in p-cresol releases electrons by the +I effect and hyperconjugation, which destabilises the phenoxide ion.
p-Cresol is therefore less acidic than phenol.
Both nitrophenols are more acidic than phenol.
solution.why_not_others: m-Nitrophenol ($pK_a$ 8.3) and o-nitrophenol ($pK_a$ 7.2) are stronger acids than phenol ($pK_a$ 10), and phenol is stronger than p-cresol.
solution.common_trap: Choosing m-nitrophenol because the meta nitro group has only a weak effect. A weak electron-withdrawing effect still increases acidity.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Phenols: acidic nature
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol.
statements.R: Delocalisation of charge is more effective in phenol than in the phenoxide ion, because resonance in phenol involves no charge separation.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by charge delocalisation, which is more effective than delocalisation in phenol, where resonance involves charge separation.
steps: A is true: the $pK_a$ of phenol is about 10, against about 15.9 for ethanol.
R reverses the fact. Resonance in phenol requires charge separation, so delocalisation is more effective in the phenoxide ion.
Hence R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: Because R is false, options 1 and 2 are ruled out. Because A is true, option 4 is ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Not noticing that R swaps phenol and phenoxide.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Phenols: acidic nature
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: o-Nitrophenol is more acidic than p-nitrophenol because the nitro group is closer to the $-OH$ group.
statements.II: A nitro group at the meta position increases the acidity of phenol more than one at the para position, because at the meta position it acts through the -R effect.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: p-Nitrophenol (7.1) > o-nitrophenol (7.2) > m-nitrophenol (8.3) in acidity. A meta $-NO_2$ acts only through the -I effect.
steps: Statement I: intramolecular H-bonding makes o-nitrophenol slightly weaker than the para isomer, so Statement I is incorrect.
Statement II: a meta $-NO_2$ cannot exert the -R effect and acts only by the -I effect, so it raises acidity less than a para $-NO_2$. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Each statement contradicts the known order of acidity, so no option that marks either statement as correct can be right.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that proximity of the nitro group to OH always means greater acidity.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Electrophilic substitution of phenols: halogenation, nitration and sulphonation
questions.question: When phenol is treated with bromine water, the product obtained is

solution.key_concept: In a polar solvent, phenol ionises to the strongly activating phenoxide ion and undergoes tribromination without any Lewis acid.
steps: Water increases ionisation of phenol to phenoxide, which is even more activating than phenol.
Bromine substitutes all the ortho and para positions.
The product, $C_6H_2Br_3OH$, separates as a white precipitate.
solution.why_not_others: Monobromophenols form only with $Br_2$ in $CS_2$ or $CHCl_3$ at low temperature. Bromobenzene would require replacement of the OH group, which does not occur.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the bromine water reaction with mono-bromination in $CS_2$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Electrophilic substitution of phenols: halogenation, nitration and sulphonation
questions.question: Nitration of phenol with dilute $HNO_3$ at 298 K gives a mixture of o- and p-nitrophenol. Which statement correctly describes how they are separated?
options: By steam distillation; the para isomer distils over because of intramolecular H-bonding
By steam distillation; the ortho isomer distils over because of intramolecular H-bonding
By steam distillation; the ortho isomer distils over because of intermolecular H-bonding
By steam distillation; the para isomer distils over because of intermolecular H-bonding

solution.key_concept: Intramolecular H-bonding prevents molecular association and makes o-nitrophenol steam volatile.
steps: In o-nitrophenol, the OH group forms an H-bond with the adjacent $NO_2$ group within the same molecule.
As a result, its molecules do not associate with each other, and it is volatile in steam.
p-Nitrophenol is intermolecularly H-bonded, so it is less volatile and remains behind.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): By steam distillation; the ortho isomer distils over because of intramolecular H-bonding
solution.why_not_others: The para isomer cannot form an intramolecular H-bond, which rules out option 1. Intermolecular H-bonding lowers volatility rather than raising it, which rules out options 3 and 4.
solution.common_trap: Interchanging the terms intramolecular and intermolecular.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Electrophilic substitution of phenols: halogenation, nitration and sulphonation
questions.question: Phenol is heated with conc. $H_2SO_4$ at about 373 K. What is the major product?

solution.key_concept: Sulphonation of phenol is kinetically controlled near room temperature (ortho product) and thermodynamically controlled at about 373 K (para product).
steps: OH is an ortho/para director, so the meta product is ruled out.
Near room temperature, the ortho isomer dominates (kinetic control).
At about 373 K, the para isomer is the major product (thermodynamic control).
solution.why_not_others: The ortho isomer is the low-temperature product. The meta position is not activated by OH. Picric acid requires nitration.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up which temperature favours the ortho isomer and which favours the para isomer.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Electrophilic substitution of phenols: halogenation, nitration and sulphonation
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

solution.key_concept: The product of electrophilic substitution in phenol depends on the solvent and on the concentration of the reagent.
steps: A: a low-polarity solvent at low temperature gives mono-bromination, mainly para, so A-II.
B: bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol, so B-III.
C: dilute $HNO_3$ gives o- and p-nitrophenol, so C-IV.
D: conc. $HNO_3$ gives picric acid, so D-I.
solution.why_not_others: Options 1 and 4 swap the two bromination products. Options 3 and 4 swap the dilute and concentrated $HNO_3$ products.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that bromination always gives the tribromo product, whatever the solvent.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Electrophilic substitution of phenols: halogenation, nitration and sulphonation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about electrophilic substitution in phenol are correct?

statements.A: The $-OH$ group activates the ring and directs incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions through its +R effect.
statements.B: Bromination of phenol requires a Lewis acid such as $FeBr_3$.
statements.C: In bromine water, the increased ionisation of phenol to the more activating phenoxide ion leads to tribromination.
statements.D: Picric acid is better prepared by sulphonation of phenol followed by nitration, because this gives a higher yield.
statements.E: Sulphonation of phenol near room temperature gives mainly p-phenolsulphonic acid.

solution.key_concept: OH is a strongly activating, ortho/para-directing group. Phenol needs no Lewis acid for halogenation, and sulphonation shows temperature control.
steps: A is true: OH activates the ring by the +R effect.
B is false: the ring is so activated that no Lewis acid is needed.
C is true: the polar solvent promotes formation of the phenoxide ion, leading to 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
D is true: sulphonation followed by nitration gives picric acid in better yield.
E is false: near room temperature the ortho isomer is the major product.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options 2 and 3 include a false statement (B or E). Option 4 leaves out the true statement D.
solution.common_trap: Carrying the benzene halogenation conditions (Lewis acid catalyst) over to phenol.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Reimer-Tiemann reaction
questions.question: Phenol is heated with chloroform and aqueous $NaOH$ at about 340 K, and the mixture is then acidified. What is the major organic product?

solution.key_concept: The Reimer-Tiemann reaction introduces a -CHO group mainly at the ortho position of phenol.
steps: $CHCl_3$ and aqueous $NaOH$ generate dichlorocarbene, $:CCl_2$.
$:CCl_2$ attacks the phenoxide ion mainly at the ortho position.
Alkaline hydrolysis of the $-CHCl_2$ intermediate followed by acidification gives $o-HOC_6H_4CHO$.
solution.why_not_others: Benzaldehyde has lost the -OH group, which does not happen. The para isomer is not the major product. Salicylic acid is formed only when $CCl_4$ is used instead of $CHCl_3$.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the $CHCl_3$ product (salicylaldehyde) with the $CCl_4$ product (salicylic acid).
solution.time_saving_tip: CHCl3 gives CHO; CCl4 gives COOH; both enter at the ortho position.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Reimer-Tiemann reaction
questions.question: Which species is the electrophile that attacks the aromatic ring in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction of phenol?

solution.key_concept: Base removes HCl from chloroform to give dichlorocarbene, which is an electron-deficient electrophile.
steps: $CHCl_3 + OH^- \rightarrow :CCl_2 + H_2O + Cl^-$
$:CCl_2$ is electron deficient and attacks the electron-rich phenoxide ring, mainly at the ortho position.
solution.why_not_others: $^+CHCl_2$ is not formed under these basic conditions. $Cl^+$ would chlorinate the ring, not formylate it. $^-CCl_3$ is negatively charged, so it cannot act as an electrophile.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that, because a base is used, the attacking species must be anionic.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Reimer-Tiemann reaction
questions.question: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction of phenol, chloroform is replaced by carbon tetrachloride and the other conditions are kept the same (aqueous $NaOH$, then acidification). What is the major product?

solution.key_concept: With $CCl_4$, the Reimer-Tiemann reaction gives a carboxylic acid group at the ortho position instead of an aldehyde group.
steps: With $CCl_4$, the carbon introduced at the ortho position carries three chlorine atoms.
Hydrolysis of this group gives -COOH rather than -CHO.
Acidification then gives 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid).
solution.why_not_others: Salicylaldehyde is the product with $CHCl_3$. Benzoic acid lacks the phenolic -OH, which is retained. Ring chlorination is not the outcome of this reaction.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the product does not change when $CHCl_3$ is replaced by $CCl_4$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Reimer-Tiemann reaction
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, the reaction mixture must be acidified at the end to obtain free salicylaldehyde.
statements.R: Dichlorocarbene, the attacking species in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, is an electron-deficient electrophile.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: In alkali, the product exists as its phenoxide, so acid is needed to liberate free salicylaldehyde.
steps: In aqueous $NaOH$, the hydroxy aldehyde stays as the sodium phenoxide, so A is true.
$:CCl_2$ is an electron-deficient electrophile, so R is true.
The need for acidification comes from the phenoxide form of the product, not from the electrophilic nature of the carbene. So R does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: R describes the attacking species, while A concerns the work-up step. They are separate facts, so option (1) is wrong. Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Marking option (1) simply because both statements are true and refer to the same reaction.
solution.time_saving_tip: Ask whether R answers 'why' for A. Here it does not.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Reimer-Tiemann reaction
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, base removes HCl from chloroform to form dichlorocarbene, which attacks the phenoxide ion mainly at the ortho position.
statements.II: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, the $-CHCl_2$ group of the intermediate is converted into the $-CHO$ group only when acid is added at the end.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Alkali, not acid, hydrolyses the benzal chloride intermediate. Acid only liberates the phenol from its phenoxide.
steps: Statement I correctly describes how $:CCl_2$ is generated and where it attacks, so it is correct.
The $-CHCl_2$ (benzal chloride type) group is hydrolysed to -CHO by the alkali already present.
The aldehyde remains as its phenoxide until acid is added, so acid is not what converts $-CHCl_2$ to -CHO. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II assigns the hydrolysis step to the acid, which is wrong. This rules out options (1) and (4). Statement I is fully correct, which rules out option (2).
solution.common_trap: Thinking the final acid step performs the hydrolysis, when it only protonates the phenoxide.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Ethers: structure
questions.question: What is the approximate C–O–C bond angle in dimethyl ether?

solution.key_concept: The oxygen in an ether is sp3 hybridised. Repulsion between the bulky alkyl groups widens the bond angle slightly beyond the tetrahedral value.
steps: The oxygen is sp3 hybridised with two lone pairs, giving a bent shape.
Repulsion between the two methyl groups widens the angle to about $111.7^\circ$.
solution.why_not_others: $104.5^\circ$ is the bond angle in water. $109.5^\circ$ is the ideal tetrahedral angle. $120^\circ$ corresponds to sp2 hybridisation.
solution.common_trap: Expecting lone-pair repulsion to shrink the angle below $109.5^\circ$, as in water.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Ethers: structure
questions.question: What are the products when anisole ($C_6H_5OCH_3$) is heated with HI?

solution.key_concept: HI cleaves the O–alkyl bond of an alkyl aryl ether, because the Ar–O bond has partial double-bond character.
steps: Delocalisation of the oxygen lone pair into the ring strengthens the Ar–O bond.
The O–$CH_3$ bond therefore breaks instead.
$C_6H_5OCH_3 + HI \rightarrow C_6H_5OH + CH_3I$
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (3) require the strong Ar–O bond to break. Option (2) shows methane, which is not formed in HI cleavage.
solution.common_trap: Writing iodobenzene and methanol by breaking the wrong C–O bond.
solution.time_saving_tip: In aryl alkyl ethers, the iodine always goes to the alkyl group.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Ethers: structure
questions.question: Ethers have boiling points close to those of alkanes of similar molar mass, yet their solubility in water is comparable to that of alcohols. Which explanation best accounts for both observations?
options: Ether molecules cannot form H-bonds with each other, but they can accept H-bonds from water molecules
Ethers are non-polar molecules with zero dipole moment
The oxygen atom in ethers is sp2 hybridised and has no lone pairs available
Ether molecules donate H-bonds to water through hydrogen atoms bonded to oxygen

solution.key_concept: Ethers have no O–H bond, so there is no intermolecular H-bonding between ether molecules. Their oxygen lone pairs can still accept H-bonds from water.
steps: With no H-bonding between ether molecules, their boiling points stay low, close to those of alkanes.
The oxygen lone pairs accept H-bonds from water molecules, which gives them alcohol-like solubility.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Ether molecules cannot form H-bonds with each other, but they can accept H-bonds from water molecules
solution.why_not_others: Ethers are bent and have a net dipole moment. Their oxygen is sp3 hybridised and carries two lone pairs. Ethers have no H attached to O, so they cannot donate H-bonds.
solution.common_trap: Assuming ethers are non-polar because they have low boiling points.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Ethers: structure
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Products of heating anisole with HI

solution.key_concept: These are the key structural data for ethers and the cleavage of an aryl alkyl ether.
steps: The C–O–C angle in dimethyl ether is about $111.7^\circ$, so A-III.
The C–O bond length is about 141 pm, so B-I.
The oxygen is sp3 hybridised, so C-II.
Anisole with HI gives $C_6H_5OH + CH_3I$, so D-IV.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps the bond angle and the bond length. Option (2) swaps the hybridisation and the products. Option (3) swaps the hybridisation and the bond angle.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the numerical values 141 and 111.7 because both are close to 100 or more.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Ethers: structure
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the structure of ethers are correct?

statements.A: The C–O–C bond angle in dimethyl ether is greater than the tetrahedral angle because of repulsion between the alkyl groups.
statements.B: Ethers have zero dipole moment because the two C–O bond dipoles cancel each other.
statements.C: In anisole, the Ar–O bond is shorter because the oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, giving the bond partial double-bond character.
statements.D: When anisole is heated with HI, the Ar–O bond is broken.
statements.E: The oxygen atom of an ether carries two lone pairs.

solution.key_concept: Ethers have a bent, sp3 oxygen. In aryl alkyl ethers, the Ar–O bond has partial double-bond character.
steps: A is correct: the angle is about $111.7^\circ$ because of alkyl group repulsion.
B is incorrect: the bent shape gives ethers a net dipole moment.
C is correct: lone-pair delocalisation shortens the Ar–O bond.
D is incorrect: the O–alkyl bond breaks, giving phenol and $CH_3I$.
E is correct: the sp3 oxygen carries two lone pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) includes B, which is false. Option (2) includes D, which is false. Option (4) leaves out C, which is true.
solution.common_trap: Treating an ether as linear and symmetric, and therefore non-polar.
solution.time_saving_tip: Eliminate any option containing B or D first.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldehydes and ketones: nature of the carbonyl group
questions.question: What are the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon in an aldehyde and the arrangement of its three sigma bonds?
options: sp2; trigonal planar with bond angles of about $120^\circ$
sp3; tetrahedral with bond angles of about $109.5^\circ$
sp; linear with a bond angle of $180^\circ$
sp2; pyramidal with bond angles of about $107^\circ$

solution.key_concept: The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised, and its three sigma bonds lie in one plane.
steps: Three sp2 orbitals form sigma bonds at about $120^\circ$ in one plane.
The remaining unhybridised p orbital overlaps with an oxygen p orbital to form the π bond.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): sp2; trigonal planar with bond angles of about $120^\circ$
solution.why_not_others: sp3 tetrahedral geometry describes the carbon after nucleophilic addition. sp is linear and is not the case here. Pyramidal geometry does not arise from sp2 hybridisation.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the geometry of the carbonyl compound with that of the tetrahedral addition intermediate.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldehydes and ketones: nature of the carbonyl group
questions.question: Propan-1-ol, propanal and butane have comparable molar masses. Which option arranges them in decreasing order of boiling point?

solution.key_concept: For compounds of similar molar mass, the boiling point order is alcohols > aldehydes/ketones > ethers ≈ alkanes.
steps: Propan-1-ol forms intermolecular H-bonds, so it has the highest boiling point.
Propanal has strong dipole-dipole attractions but no H-bonding, so it comes next.
Butane has only weak forces, so it has the lowest boiling point.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) places the aldehyde above the H-bonded alcohol. Option (3) reverses the order. Option (4) ignores the dipole-dipole attraction in propanal.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the high dipole moment of the carbonyl group outweighs H-bonding in alcohols.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldehydes and ketones: nature of the carbonyl group
questions.question: Which statement about the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones is correct?
options: The C=O double bond consists of two π bonds
The carbonyl carbon is an electrophilic (Lewis acid) site and the oxygen is a nucleophilic (Lewis base) site
Aldehydes and ketones have smaller dipole moments than ethers
The oxygen of the carbonyl group is the electrophilic centre because it is more electronegative

solution.key_concept: Because the C=O bond is polarised as $>C^{\delta+}=O^{\delta-}$, the carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen is nucleophilic.
steps: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so electron density shifts towards oxygen.
The dipolar resonance form $>C^+–O^-$ shows the carbon as electron deficient (a Lewis acid site) and the oxygen as electron rich (a Lewis base site).
solution.final_answer: Option (2): The carbonyl carbon is an electrophilic (Lewis acid) site and the oxygen is a nucleophilic (Lewis base) site
solution.why_not_others: C=O consists of one σ bond and one π bond. Carbonyl compounds have larger dipole moments than ethers. The electronegative oxygen carries partial negative charge, so it is nucleophilic, not electrophilic.
solution.common_trap: Linking high electronegativity with electrophilic character.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldehydes and ketones: nature of the carbonyl group
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Lower aldehydes and ketones are miscible with water.
statements.R: Molecules of aldehydes and ketones form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with one another.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Carbonyl compounds have no O–H bond. They can accept H-bonds from water but cannot H-bond with each other.
steps: Lower aldehydes and ketones dissolve in water by accepting H-bonds from water, so A is true.
With no H on oxygen, they cannot form H-bonds among their own molecules; only dipole-dipole forces act between them. So R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, which rules out options (1), (2) and (4).
solution.common_trap: Assuming that being able to H-bond with water means the molecules also H-bond with each other.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldehydes and ketones: nature of the carbonyl group
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Because the carbonyl group is trigonal planar, a nucleophile can attack the carbonyl carbon from only one face of the group.
statements.II: The C=O bond is best described as a resonance hybrid of the neutral form and the dipolar form $>C^+–O^-$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: The planar carbonyl group can be approached from either face. Its polarity is shown by the dipolar resonance form.
steps: Planar geometry leaves both faces open, so nucleophiles can attack from either face. Statement I is incorrect.
The C=O bond is a hybrid of $>C=O$ and $>C^+–O^-$. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I contradicts the either-face attack allowed by planar geometry, which rules out options (1) and (3). Statement II is true, which rules out option (2).
solution.common_trap: Thinking that planarity restricts the direction of attack, when it actually opens both faces.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Nucleophilic addition to C=O: HCN, NH3 and its derivatives; Grignard reagent
questions.question: A ketone is treated with a Grignard reagent ($RMgX$) and the product is then hydrolysed. Which class of compound is obtained?

solution.key_concept: In Grignard addition, HCHO gives a 1° alcohol, RCHO gives a 2° alcohol and $R_2CO$ gives a 3° alcohol.
steps: $R^-$ adds to the carbonyl carbon, which already carries two alkyl groups.
Hydrolysis gives a carbon bearing three alkyl groups and an -OH group, which is a 3° alcohol.
solution.why_not_others: A primary alcohol comes from HCHO. A secondary alcohol comes from other aldehydes. An aldehyde is not a product of Grignard addition.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the products obtained from aldehydes and from ketones.
solution.time_saving_tip: Count the groups on the carbonyl carbon and add one; that gives the alcohol's degree.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Nucleophilic addition to C=O: HCN, NH3 and its derivatives; Grignard reagent
questions.question: The addition of HCN to aldehydes and ketones is catalysed by a base. What is the role of the base?
options: It generates $CN^-$, which is a stronger nucleophile than HCN
It protonates the carbonyl oxygen and makes the carbon more electrophilic
It converts the carbonyl compound into its enolate, which then reacts with HCN
It removes the water eliminated during cyanohydrin formation

solution.key_concept: In cyanohydrin formation, the true nucleophile is $CN^-$.
steps: The base removes a proton from HCN to give $CN^-$.
$CN^-$ attacks the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide that is then protonated to form the cyanohydrin $>C(OH)CN$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): It generates $CN^-$, which is a stronger nucleophile than HCN
solution.why_not_others: A base cannot protonate anything. The reaction involves no enolate. No water is eliminated in cyanohydrin formation.
solution.common_trap: Confusing cyanohydrin formation with the addition-elimination reactions of ammonia derivatives.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Nucleophilic addition to C=O: HCN, NH3 and its derivatives; Grignard reagent
questions.question: Acetone reacts with semicarbazide ($NH_2NHCONH_2$) in weakly acidic medium. What is the product formed?

solution.key_concept: In semicarbazide, only the $NH_2$ group not attached to C=O acts as the nucleophile. Addition is followed by elimination of water.
steps: The $NH_2$ attached to the C=O of the amide is deactivated, so the terminal $NH_2$ of the $–NHNH_2$ end attacks.
The tetrahedral intermediate loses $H_2O$ to form $>C=N–Z$.
The product is the semicarbazone $(CH_3)_2C=N–NHCONH_2$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) results from attack by the amide $NH_2$, which is not nucleophilic. Option (2) stops before water is eliminated. Option (3) is a hydrazone, the product formed with hydrazine.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that either $NH_2$ group of semicarbazide can act as the nucleophile.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Nucleophilic addition to C=O: HCN, NH3 and its derivatives; Grignard reagent
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Carbonyl compound + HCN in the presence of base

solution.key_concept: Each nucleophile gives a characteristic addition or addition-elimination product.
steps: Hydroxylamine gives an oxime, so A-III.
Phenylhydrazine gives a phenylhydrazone, so B-IV.
$6HCHO + 4NH_3 \rightarrow (CH_2)_6N_4 + 6H_2O$, so C-I.
HCN with a base gives a cyanohydrin, so D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps the oxime and the phenylhydrazone. Option (2) swaps urotropine and the cyanohydrin. Option (3) swaps the oxime and urotropine.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that formaldehyde with ammonia gives the cage compound urotropine.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Nucleophilic addition to C=O: HCN, NH3 and its derivatives; Grignard reagent
questions.question: Which of the following statements about nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group are correct?

statements.A: During nucleophilic addition, the carbonyl carbon changes from sp2 to sp3 hybridisation.
statements.B: Reactions of carbonyl compounds with ammonia derivatives work best in strongly acidic medium, at a pH of about 1.
statements.C: Formaldehyde reacts with $CH_3MgBr$, followed by hydrolysis, to give a primary alcohol.
statements.D: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine gives orange-yellow 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazones with both aldehydes and ketones.
statements.E: Acetaldehyde reacts with a Grignard reagent, followed by hydrolysis, to give a tertiary alcohol.

solution.key_concept: This combines the hybridisation change on addition, the pH needed for ammonia derivatives, the Grignard alcohol classes and the 2,4-DNP test.
steps: A is correct: the planar sp2 carbon becomes a tetrahedral sp3 carbon.
B is incorrect: the optimum pH is about 3.5, because a strongly acidic medium protonates the nucleophile.
C is correct: HCHO gives a 1° alcohol (here ethanol).
D is correct: 2,4-DNP gives a positive test with both aldehydes and ketones.
E is incorrect: aldehydes other than HCHO give 2° alcohols.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (4) include B, which is false. Options (2) and (4) include E, which is false.
solution.common_trap: Believing that more acid always speeds up the reaction with ammonia derivatives, or that 2,4-DNP distinguishes aldehydes from ketones.
solution.time_saving_tip: Spotting B and E as false leaves only option (3).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Relative reactivities of aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Which of the following compounds is the most reactive towards nucleophilic addition?

solution.key_concept: Reactivity towards nucleophilic addition falls as more, and larger, electron-releasing alkyl groups are attached to the carbonyl carbon.
steps: HCHO has no alkyl group. Its carbonyl carbon is the least hindered and the most electron-deficient.
$CH_3CHO$ has one alkyl group, so it is less reactive than HCHO.
The ketones $CH_3COCH_3$ and $C_2H_5COCH_3$ have two alkyl groups each, so they are less reactive still.
Order: HCHO > $CH_3CHO$ > $CH_3COCH_3$ > $C_2H_5COCH_3$.
solution.why_not_others: $CH_3CHO$ has one electron-releasing methyl group. Both ketones have two alkyl groups, which add steric hindrance and reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a larger aldehyde or ketone is more reactive. More and bulkier alkyl groups lower the reactivity.
solution.time_saving_tip: Count the alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon. The fewer there are, the more reactive the compound.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Relative reactivities of aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Choose the correct decreasing order of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition for p-nitrobenzaldehyde (P), benzaldehyde (B), p-tolualdehyde (T) and p-methoxybenzaldehyde (M).

solution.key_concept: An electron-withdrawing group on the ring increases the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon. An electron-donating group decreases it.
steps: $-NO_2$ is electron-withdrawing, so P is the most reactive.
Benzaldehyde has no substituent and comes next.
$-CH_3$ is a weak electron donor, so T is less reactive than B.
$-OCH_3$ is a stronger electron donor, so M is the least reactive.
Order: P > B > T > M.
solution.why_not_others: M > T > B > P is the exact reverse of the correct order. B > P > T > M ignores the activating effect of $-NO_2$. P > T > B > M wrongly treats $-CH_3$ as activating.
solution.common_trap: Treating every substituent as activating. Electron-donating groups such as $-CH_3$ and $-OCH_3$ reduce reactivity.
solution.time_saving_tip: Withdrawing groups raise reactivity and donating groups lower it. Unsubstituted benzaldehyde sits between them.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Relative reactivities of aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Propanal is more reactive than benzaldehyde towards nucleophilic addition. The best explanation is that
options: the benzene ring donates electrons to the carbonyl group by resonance, reducing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon in benzaldehyde
the benzene ring withdraws electrons from the carbonyl group, making benzaldehyde less polar
benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so its carbonyl carbon cannot be attacked by nucleophiles
propanal has two electron-releasing alkyl groups on its carbonyl carbon

solution.key_concept: In aromatic aldehydes, resonance with the ring reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.
steps: The phenyl ring is conjugated with the C=O group.
Resonance donates electron density from the ring to the carbonyl group.
This lowers the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, so benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): the benzene ring donates electrons to the carbonyl group by resonance, reducing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon in benzaldehyde
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) gives the wrong direction of electron flow. Option (3) confuses α-H acidity with nucleophilic addition; the absence of α-H does not stop addition. Option (4) is false because propanal, an aldehyde, has only one alkyl group on its carbonyl carbon.
solution.common_trap: Linking the absence of α-H to low reactivity in nucleophilic addition.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Relative reactivities of aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Acetaldehyde is more reactive than acetone towards nucleophilic addition.
statements.R: The methyl groups in acetone are electron-withdrawing and increase the positive charge on its carbonyl carbon.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Alkyl groups are electron-releasing. They reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon and also add steric hindrance.
steps: Acetaldehyde has one alkyl group and acetone has two, so A is true.
Methyl groups release electrons. They reduce, not increase, the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, so R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R reverses the electronic effect of alkyl groups. Every option that treats R as true is therefore wrong.
solution.common_trap: Confusing electron-releasing alkyl groups with electron-withdrawing groups.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Relative reactivities of aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Di-tert-butyl ketone is more reactive than acetone towards nucleophilic addition because its bulky alkyl groups release more electrons.
statements.II: p-Tolualdehyde is less reactive than benzaldehyde towards nucleophilic addition because the $-CH_3$ group donates electrons to the ring.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Bulky groups and electron-donating groups both lower carbonyl reactivity.
steps: Bulky tert-butyl groups hinder the approach of the nucleophile and also release electrons. Di-tert-butyl ketone is therefore very unreactive, so Statement I is incorrect.
$-CH_3$ is an electron-donating group, so p-tolualdehyde is less reactive than benzaldehyde. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I wrongly treats greater electron release as an increase in reactivity, and it ignores steric hindrance.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that more electron release makes the carbonyl carbon more reactive. It does the opposite.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxidation and reduction: Wolff-Kishner and Clemmensen
questions.question: The reagent used in the Clemmensen reduction of a ketone to a hydrocarbon is
options: $NH_2NH_2$, then $KOH$ in ethylene glycol with heat

solution.key_concept: Clemmensen reduction converts C=O into $CH_2$ in an acidic medium.
steps: Clemmensen reduction uses zinc amalgam with conc. HCl.
It converts $>C=O$ into $>CH_2$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) is the Wolff-Kishner reagent. $NaBH_4$ gives alcohols, not hydrocarbons. $H_2$ with $Pd/BaSO_4$ is not the Clemmensen reagent.
solution.common_trap: Interchanging the Clemmensen (acidic) and Wolff-Kishner (basic) reagents.
solution.time_saving_tip: Clemmensen and conc. HCl both fit the acidic medium.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxidation and reduction: Wolff-Kishner and Clemmensen
questions.question: A ketone also contains a group that decomposes in acid but is stable in base. Which method is most suitable for converting its C=O group into $CH_2$ without affecting the other group?
options: Wolff-Kishner reduction with $NH_2NH_2$, then $KOH$ in ethylene glycol with heat

solution.key_concept: Choose the C=O to $CH_2$ method according to the acid or base sensitivity of the other groups.
steps: The product must contain $CH_2$, so a complete reduction is needed, not reduction to an alcohol.
The other group is acid-sensitive, so Clemmensen reduction (conc. HCl) cannot be used.
Wolff-Kishner reduction works in a basic medium, so it is suitable.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Wolff-Kishner reduction with $NH_2NH_2$, then $KOH$ in ethylene glycol with heat
solution.why_not_others: Clemmensen reduction uses acid, which would destroy the acid-sensitive group. $NaBH_4$ and $LiAlH_4$ reduce a ketone only to a 2° alcohol.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $NaBH_4$ or $LiAlH_4$ for the C=O to $CH_2$ change. They stop at the alcohol stage.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxidation and reduction: Wolff-Kishner and Clemmensen
questions.question: Pent-4-enal, $CH_2=CHCH_2CH_2CHO$, is treated with $NaBH_4$. The product is

solution.key_concept: $NaBH_4$ reduces aldehydes to 1° alcohols but does not reduce an isolated C=C bond.
steps: The $-CHO$ group is reduced to $-CH_2OH$.
The isolated C=C bond is not affected by $NaBH_4$.
Product: $CH_2=CHCH_2CH_2CH_2OH$, which is pent-4-en-1-ol.
solution.why_not_others: Pentan-1-ol would require reduction of the C=C bond as well. Pent-1-ene would come from a complete C=O to $CH_2$ reduction such as Clemmensen or Wolff-Kishner. Pent-4-enoic acid is an oxidation product, not a reduction product.
solution.common_trap: Assuming $NaBH_4$ also saturates the C=C bond.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxidation and reduction: Wolff-Kishner and Clemmensen
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Oxidation of an aldehyde with Tollens' reagent

solution.key_concept: Learn the medium and the product for each oxidation and reduction method.
steps: Clemmensen reduction uses $Zn-Hg$ and conc. HCl in an acidic medium: A-III.
Wolff-Kishner reduction goes through the hydrazone, then KOH in ethylene glycol, releasing $N_2$: B-I.
$NaBH_4$ reduces a ketone to a 2° alcohol: C-II.
Tollens' reagent oxidises an aldehyde to the acid: D-IV.
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings swap Clemmensen with Wolff-Kishner, swap the alcohol with the acid, or do both.
solution.common_trap: Interchanging the acidic and basic reduction methods.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxidation and reduction: Wolff-Kishner and Clemmensen
questions.question: Which of the following statements about oxidation and reduction of carbonyl compounds are correct?

statements.A: Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids even by mild oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent.
statements.B: Ketones are oxidised only under vigorous conditions, with C–C bond cleavage giving acids with fewer carbon atoms.
statements.D: Both Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reductions convert a C=O group into $CH_2$, giving a hydrocarbon.
statements.E: $NaBH_4$ reduces an isolated C=C bond along with the C=O group.

options: A, B, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Aldehydes are easily oxidised and ketones are not. Hydride reagents give alcohols, while Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reductions give hydrocarbons.
steps: A is true: mild agents oxidise aldehydes.
B is true: ketones need strong oxidants and undergo C–C cleavage.
C is false: ketones give 2° alcohols, not 1° alcohols.
D is true: both methods convert C=O into $CH_2$.
E is false: $NaBH_4$ does not reduce an isolated C=C bond.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes C or E, which are false, or leaves out a true statement.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that ketones give primary alcohols on reduction.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rule out C first. Every option containing C is then eliminated.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Acidity of alpha-hydrogen
questions.question: Which of the following compounds has no α-hydrogen?

solution.key_concept: An α-carbon bearing three alkyl groups has no hydrogen.
steps: In $(CH_3)_3CCHO$, the carbon next to CHO is quaternary, so there is no α-H.
Each of the other compounds has at least one H on the α-carbon.
solution.why_not_others: $CH_3CHO$ has 3 α-H, $CH_3COCH_3$ has 6 α-H, and $(CH_3)_2CHCHO$ has 1 α-H on the isopropyl carbon.
solution.common_trap: Assuming an isopropyl α-carbon has no α-H. It still has one.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Acidity of alpha-hydrogen
questions.question: Which of the following hydrogens is the most acidic?
options: A hydrogen of the $CH_2$ group in $CH_3COCH_2COCH_3$

solution.key_concept: A hydrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups is much more acidic ($pK_a$ about 9–11) than an ordinary α-H.
steps: Ethane hydrogens have $pK_a$ about 50.
Hydrogens α to a single C=O group, such as those in acetone, have $pK_a$ about 19–20.
The $CH_2$ group between the two C=O groups of a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound has $pK_a$ about 9–11, so it is the most acidic.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A hydrogen of the $CH_2$ group in $CH_3COCH_2COCH_3$
solution.why_not_others: The terminal methyl hydrogens of $CH_3COCH_2COCH_3$ are α to only one C=O group, like those of acetone. Ethane has no carbonyl group at all.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every hydrogen in a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound is equally acidic.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Acidity of alpha-hydrogen
questions.question: How many α-hydrogens are present in 2,2-dimethylpentan-3-one, $(CH_3)_3C-CO-CH_2CH_3$?

solution.key_concept: α-Hydrogens are only those attached directly to a carbon adjacent to the C=O group.
steps: One α-carbon is the tert-butyl carbon, which is quaternary and has 0 H.
The other α-carbon is the $CH_2$ of the ethyl group, which has 2 H.
Total α-H = 2.
solution.why_not_others: 11 counts the nine tert-butyl methyl hydrogens as α. 5 counts all the ethyl hydrogens. 3 counts the terminal $CH_3$ hydrogens, which are β.
solution.common_trap: Treating the methyl hydrogens of a tert-butyl group as α-hydrogens.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Acidity of alpha-hydrogen
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Benzophenone, $C_6H_5COC_6H_5$, cannot form an enolate ion.
statements.R: A hydrogen lying between two carbonyl groups in a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound is more acidic than an α-hydrogen of acetone.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Enolate formation requires an α-H. Two carbonyl groups increase α-H acidity.
steps: Both α-carbons of benzophenone are ring carbons that carry no H, so it has no α-H. A is true.
1,3-dicarbonyl compounds have $pK_a$ about 9–11, compared with about 19–20 for acetone. R is true.
A follows from the absence of α-H, not from the acidity of 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds. R does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) are wrong. R does not explain A, so option (1) is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Choosing option (1) just because both statements concern α-H acidity.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Acidity of alpha-hydrogen
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In 2,2-dimethylpropanal, $(CH_3)_3CCHO$, the α-carbon carries one hydrogen, so the compound undergoes aldol condensation with dilute NaOH.
statements.II: In the enolate ion of acetone, the negative charge is shared between the α-carbon and the oxygen atom by resonance.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Enolate formation needs an α-H, and the enolate is stabilised by resonance.
steps: The α-carbon of $(CH_3)_3CCHO$ carries three methyl groups and no H. It cannot form an enolate, so it does not undergo aldol condensation. Statement I is incorrect.
In the enolate, the negative charge is delocalised between the α-carbon and the oxygen. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I miscounts the α-hydrogens.
solution.common_trap: Confusing tert-butyl (no α-H) with isopropyl (one α-H).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldol condensation, Cannizzaro reaction and haloform reaction
questions.question: Ethanal is treated with dilute NaOH and the product is then heated. The final organic product is

solution.key_concept: On heating, the aldol loses water to give an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde.
steps: Dilute NaOH gives the aldol, $CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO$.
Heating removes $H_2O$, giving $CH_3CH=CHCHO$, which is but-2-enal.
solution.why_not_others: 3-Hydroxybutanal is the product before heating. Ethanol and sodium ethanoate would be Cannizzaro-type products, which do not form because ethanal has α-H. Butanal is a saturated aldehyde and does not form.
solution.common_trap: Stopping at the aldol stage even though heating is specified.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldol condensation, Cannizzaro reaction and haloform reaction
questions.question: A mixture of formaldehyde and benzaldehyde is heated with concentrated NaOH. The main products are

solution.key_concept: In crossed Cannizzaro reaction, HCHO is always the molecule oxidised, to formate.
steps: Neither aldehyde has an α-H, so with conc. NaOH a Cannizzaro reaction occurs.
HCHO is oxidised to $HCOO^-$, which appears as sodium formate.
Benzaldehyde is reduced to $C_6H_5CH_2OH$.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Sodium formate and benzyl alcohol
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) reverses which aldehyde is oxidised and which is reduced. Options (2) and (3) show both aldehydes reduced or both oxidised, which cannot happen in a disproportionation.
solution.common_trap: Assuming benzaldehyde is the molecule oxidised in crossed Cannizzaro.
solution.time_saving_tip: In crossed Cannizzaro, HCHO always becomes formate.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldol condensation, Cannizzaro reaction and haloform reaction
questions.question: Pentan-2-one, $CH_3COCH_2CH_2CH_3$, is treated with sodium hypoiodite (NaOI). Along with iodoform, the other product is

solution.key_concept: The haloform reaction gives $RCOO^-$ with one carbon fewer than the methyl ketone $RCOCH_3$.
steps: Here R = $CH_3CH_2CH_2-$.
$RCOCH_3 + 3NaOI \rightarrow RCOONa + CHI_3 + 2NaOH$.
The product $CH_3CH_2CH_2COONa$ is sodium butanoate.
solution.why_not_others: Sodium pentanoate keeps all five carbons. Sodium propanoate and sodium ethanoate remove too many carbons.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that the carboxylate has one carbon fewer than the ketone.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldol condensation, Cannizzaro reaction and haloform reaction
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Chloroform exposed to air and light

solution.key_concept: Aldol, Cannizzaro and haloform reactions, and the oxidation of chloroform, each give characteristic products.
steps: Ethanal with dilute NaOH gives the aldol 3-hydroxybutanal: A-III.
Benzaldehyde has no α-H, so conc. NaOH gives the Cannizzaro products benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate: B-IV.
Acetone with NaOI gives iodoform and sodium acetate: C-I.
Chloroform in air and light gives phosgene and HCl: D-II.
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings swap the aldol and Cannizzaro products, or swap the haloform and phosgene products.
solution.common_trap: Giving benzaldehyde aldol products, even though it has no α-H.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldol condensation, Cannizzaro reaction and haloform reaction
questions.question: Which of the following statements about aldol, Cannizzaro and haloform reactions are correct?

statements.A: Crossed aldol condensation between ethanal and propanal gives four products.
statements.B: In the Claisen-Schmidt condensation of benzaldehyde with acetone, the E (trans) isomer of the α,β-unsaturated ketone is favoured.
statements.C: The Cannizzaro reaction is a disproportionation that requires concentrated NaOH and an aldehyde without α-hydrogen.
statements.D: When pent-3-en-2-one, $CH_3CH=CHCOCH_3$, undergoes the haloform reaction with NaOCl, its C=C bond is also cleaved.
statements.E: Ethanol gives a negative iodoform test because it is not a carbonyl compound.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept: Know the conditions and scope of aldol, Cannizzaro and haloform reactions.
steps: A is true: both aldehydes have α-H, so four crossed aldol products form.
B is true: the E alkene is favoured in Claisen-Schmidt condensation.
C is true: Cannizzaro needs conc. NaOH and no α-H, and is a disproportionation.
D is false: a C=C bond is not attacked in the haloform reaction.
E is false: ethanol gives a positive iodoform test.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and C only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes D or E, both of which are false.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that only methyl ketones give the iodoform test. Ethanol and $CH_3CH(OH)R$ alcohols also give it.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Chemical tests to distinguish aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Benzaldehyde gives a positive result with which one of the following tests?
options: Fehling's solution, giving a red-brown precipitate
Tollens' reagent, giving a silver mirror
Iodine and NaOH, giving a yellow precipitate
Benedict's solution, giving a red-brown precipitate

solution.key_concept: Tollens' reagent is reduced by all aldehydes, aliphatic and aromatic. Fehling's and Benedict's solutions respond only to aliphatic aldehydes.
steps: Benzaldehyde is an aromatic aldehyde, so it reduces Tollens' reagent and deposits a silver mirror.
Fehling's and Benedict's solutions give $Cu_2O$ only with aliphatic aldehydes, so benzaldehyde gives no precipitate.
The iodoform test needs a $CH_3CO-$ group or acetaldehyde, and $C_6H_5CHO$ has neither.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Tollens' reagent, giving a silver mirror
solution.why_not_others: Fehling's and Benedict's solutions are negative for aromatic aldehydes. The iodoform test is negative because benzaldehyde is not a methyl ketone and is not acetaldehyde.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every aldehyde reduces Fehling's or Benedict's solution.
solution.time_saving_tip: Aromatic aldehyde means Tollens' is positive and Fehling's is negative.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Chemical tests to distinguish aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Which of the following compounds gives a yellow precipitate with $I_2$/NaOH but does NOT give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?

solution.key_concept: The iodoform test is positive for methyl ketones and for acetaldehyde. Tollens' reagent is positive only for aldehydes.
steps: Propanone is a methyl ketone, so it forms yellow $CHI_3$ with $I_2$/NaOH.
Propanone is a ketone and does not reduce Tollens' reagent.
Ethanal is positive in both tests, so it fails the second condition.
Propanal and ethanoic acid are both negative in the iodoform test.
solution.why_not_others: Ethanal also gives a silver mirror. Ethanoic acid does not give the iodoform test even though it contains $CH_3CO-$. Propanal gives a silver mirror but no iodoform.
solution.common_trap: Thinking acetic acid gives the iodoform test because it contains a $CH_3CO-$ group.
solution.time_saving_tip: Iodoform positive and Tollens' negative together point to a methyl ketone.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Chemical tests to distinguish aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Which of the following reagents CANNOT be used to distinguish propanal from propanone?

solution.key_concept: 2,4-DNP gives an orange-yellow precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones. It confirms a carbonyl group but cannot tell the two classes apart.
steps: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with propanal only.
Fehling's solution gives red-brown $Cu_2O$ with propanal, an aliphatic aldehyde, but not with propanone.
$I_2$/NaOH gives yellow $CHI_3$ with propanone, a methyl ketone, but not with propanal.
2,4-DNP gives an orange-yellow precipitate with both compounds.
solution.why_not_others: Each of the other three reagents gives a positive result with only one of the two compounds, so each can distinguish them.
solution.common_trap: Assuming 2,4-DNP distinguishes aldehydes from ketones.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Chemical tests to distinguish aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Fructose reduces Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution even though it contains a ketone group.
statements.R: α-Hydroxy ketones are able to reduce Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Ketones are generally not reducing agents, but α-hydroxy ketones such as fructose reduce Tollens' and Fehling's reagents.
steps: Fructose gives a positive Tollens' test and a positive Fehling's test, so A is true.
α-Hydroxy ketones reduce both reagents, so R is true.
Fructose is an α-hydroxy ketone, so R correctly explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true and directly connected, which rules out options 2, 3 and 4.
solution.common_trap: Concluding that no compound with a ketone group can reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Chemical tests to distinguish aldehydes and ketones
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Benedict's solution gives a red-brown precipitate of $Cu_2O$ with benzaldehyde, because all aldehydes are reducing agents.
statements.II: Ethyl acetate gives a yellow precipitate of $CHI_3$ with $I_2$/NaOH, because it contains a $CH_3CO-$ group.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Benedict's and Fehling's solutions respond only to aliphatic aldehydes. The iodoform test is negative for acetic acid and its esters.
steps: Benzaldehyde is aromatic and does not respond to Benedict's solution, so Statement I is incorrect.
Esters of acetic acid do not give the iodoform test even though they contain $CH_3CO-$, so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are false, so every option that calls either one correct is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Treating every $CH_3CO-$ compound as iodoform positive, and treating every aldehyde as Fehling's or Benedict's positive.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Carboxylic acids: acidic strength and factors affecting it
questions.question: Which of the following is the strongest acid?

solution.key_concept: Acidity increases with the number of electron-withdrawing groups attached near the COOH group.
steps: Each Cl atom withdraws electron density by the -I effect and stabilises the carboxylate anion.
The order is $CCl_3COOH > CHCl_2COOH > ClCH_2COOH > CH_3COOH$.
solution.why_not_others: The other acids carry fewer Cl atoms, or none in the case of acetic acid, so their anions are less stabilised.
solution.time_saving_tip: More electronegative substituents near COOH mean a stronger acid.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Carboxylic acids: acidic strength and factors affecting it
questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct decreasing order of acidic strength?

solution.key_concept: Electron-donating alkyl groups decrease acidity. A phenyl group attached directly to COOH increases acidity.
steps: The $pK_a$ values are $HCOOH$ 3.75, $C_6H_5COOH$ 4.19 and $CH_3COOH$ 4.76.
An isopropyl group donates more electron density than a methyl group, so $(CH_3)_2CHCOOH$ is the weakest.
The decreasing order is $HCOOH > C_6H_5COOH > CH_3COOH > (CH_3)_2CHCOOH$.
solution.why_not_others: Benzoic acid is weaker than formic acid but stronger than acetic acid. Options 2, 3 and 4 misplace at least one of these acids.
solution.common_trap: Placing benzoic acid below acetic acid by ignoring the effect of the directly attached $sp^2$ phenyl group.
solution.time_saving_tip: A lower $pK_a$ means a stronger acid.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Carboxylic acids: acidic strength and factors affecting it
questions.question: Which of the following acids has the largest acid dissociation constant $K_a$?

solution.key_concept: The -I effect of a substituent weakens with distance from COOH. The closer the electron-withdrawing group, the stronger the acid.
steps: In 2-chlorobutanoic acid, Cl sits on the carbon next to COOH, so the anion is stabilised most.
The order is 2-chloro > 3-chloro > 4-chloro > butanoic acid.
The strongest acid has the largest $K_a$.
solution.why_not_others: In the 3- and 4-chloro acids the Cl is farther from COOH, so the -I effect is weaker. Butanoic acid has no electron-withdrawing group.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a larger $K_a$ means a weaker acid.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Carboxylic acids: acidic strength and factors affecting it
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: $-NO_2$ group at the para position of benzoic acid

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: $-OCH_3$ group at the para position of benzoic acid

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Negative charge delocalised onto less electronegative carbon atoms

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Two equivalent resonance structures with the charge on two oxygen atoms

solution.key_concept: Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols because of resonance in the carboxylate ion. Substituents on the benzoic acid ring change acidity through electron withdrawal or donation.
steps: Carboxylate has two equivalent resonance structures, giving A-II.
In phenoxide the charge spreads onto ring carbons, which are less electronegative, giving B-I.
p-Nitrobenzoic acid is stronger than benzoic acid, giving C-IV.
p-Methoxybenzoic acid is weaker than benzoic acid, giving D-III.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 interchanges the two ions. Option 3 interchanges the effects of the two substituents. Option 4 interchanges both pairs.
solution.common_trap: Treating $-OCH_3$ as acid-strengthening and overlooking that at the para position it decreases acidity.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Carboxylic acids: acidic strength and factors affecting it
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the acidic strength of carboxylic acids are correct?

statements.B: Phenol liberates $CO_2$ when treated with aqueous $NaHCO_3$.
statements.C: Most ortho-substituted benzoic acids are stronger acids than benzoic acid.
statements.D: p-Methoxybenzoic acid is a stronger acid than benzoic acid.
statements.E: Benzoic acid ($pK_a$ 4.19) has a larger $K_a$ than acetic acid ($pK_a$ 4.76).

solution.key_concept: Electronegativity of substituents, the ortho effect, ring substituents and $pK_a$ values together decide relative acidity.
steps: A is true because F is more electronegative than Br, so its -I effect is stronger.
B is false because phenol is weaker than carbonic acid and gives no effervescence with $NaHCO_3$.
C is true because of the ortho effect.
D is false because a para $-OCH_3$ group decreases acidity.
E is true because a lower $pK_a$ corresponds to a larger $K_a$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: The other options all include B or D, and both of those statements are false.
solution.common_trap: Thinking phenol reacts with $NaHCO_3$ to give $CO_2$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Eliminate B first. That removes option 2, and D then removes options 3 and 4.
